citation_entries.sentence: Yes, our teachers left room for doubt, and they treated doubt aimed at understanding as hunger, not as sin.
Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling, and that growing into understanding means asking.
Our word for faith, pistis, meant the soul's first real turn toward God, and it could stand beside unresolved questions.
Origen's rule was that what the apostles delivered plainly is fixed, and everything else is open ground.
Our doubters stood inside a praying community, questioned inside the rule of faith, and were expected to bring the question to a teacher.

Dionysius of Alexandria wrote, as Eusebius quotes him at VII.25: “But I could not bring myself to reject the book, since many of our people hold it in high regard. Instead, I suppose that it is beyond my understanding, and that a hidden and more wonderful meaning lies in every part. For when I do not understand, I suspect that a deeper sense lies beneath the words. I do not measure and judge them by my own reason. Leaving the greater part to faith, I regard them as too high for me to grasp. And I do not reject what I cannot comprehend. Rather, I marvel at it, because I do not understand it.”
When churches in the Arsinoite villages split over Nepos's reading of the promises, the bishop answered with three days of open argument, not a condemnation.
After Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation.
We did not have the modern language of a private crisis of faith, and the teachers' sources barely show what ordinary doubters themselves felt.

text: Yes, our teachers left room for doubt, and they treated doubt aimed at understanding as hunger, not as sin. Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling, and that growing into understanding means asking. Our word for faith, pistis, meant the soul's first real turn toward God, and it could stand beside unresolved questions. Origen's rule was that what the apostles delivered plainly is fixed, and everything else is open ground. Our doubters stood inside a praying community, questioned inside the rule of faith, and were expected to bring the question to a teacher. Dionysius of Alexandria wrote, as Eusebius quotes him at VII.25: “But I could not bring myself to reject the book, since many of our people hold it in high regard. Instead, I suppose that it is beyond my understanding, and that a hidden and more wonderful meaning lies in every part. For when I do not understand, I suspect that a deeper sense lies beneath the words. I do not measure and judge them by my own reason. Leaving the greater part to faith, I regard them as too high for me to grasp. And I do not reject what I cannot comprehend. Rather, I marvel at it, because I do not understand it.”. When churches in the Arsinoite villages split over Nepos's reading of the promises, the bishop answered with three days of open argument, not a condemnation. After Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation. We did not have the modern language of a private crisis of faith, and the teachers' sources barely show what ordinary doubters themselves felt.
